"Like a diamond in the sky"

This is probably the strangest line in the entire song. Most people don't take notice of it, they think that it's some sort of way of saying that the star is pretty like a diamond. Everyone I know thinks I'm crazy for freaking out about it, but it's just so wrong, and it stands out from the entire thing, glaring me in the face. Not only that, but it's right there IN THE FIRST VERSE! Nobody, NOBODY, should be able to miss it, yet it passes right over the heads of many.

Maybe it's because they haven't read all the verses. That's right, there's not just one, but five verses in this tale about the yet to come. Well, I hope it's not, but it probably is.

"When the blazing sun is gone"

This is what finally triggered me to really take a look at the entirety of the song. What started me on the path to finally finding it's true meaning. Sure, it looks like it's just talking about night, especially when you take into account the fourth verse, but I think that it's something deeper, or maybe shallower. It's actually referring to a time when the blazing sun is gone, and unlike how people say that it's going away in a couple million years, the sun will be going away tomorrow.

I'm so very, very, sorry. The sun will go away tomorrow, and there's nothing I can do to stop it at this point. I could attempt to destroy my research, but security would stop me before I get too far, were I to try. And besides, I need to survive, so I need to cooperate with my company at this point. Hopefully, with my help, the diamond in the sky can become the twinkling beacon star, at least for now, and hopefully become the new sun in the sky, long after the diamond shuts it's eye.

There is one other really weird thing that's been bothering me... how could he know?

I mean, this song is ancient and yet somehow the writer knew about the diamond energy creation project. I mean, this is not only supposed to be top-secret stuff to be tested out at the ISS, but it's a project that started long after the author of the song died. How could he know what to write to send me this warning? How could he know that the coordinates would be off just enough to launch our shuttle. the little star, into the sun? And how could he have figured out that our project could take out the sun? I mean, it's fortunate that the song survived from the 1800's until now, and it's interesting how he masked the warning in such a way that people think that the song's about the north star, but how did he know about what we were going to do, and what I have to do to provide the earth with the light and warmth that they'll need until a true artificial sun can be created.

The real question is: What is worse - movies based on video games, or video games based on movies?

Most of them are crap, chiefly because most directors in Hollywood are completely oblivious of video games at best or loath them at worst because the gaming industry has been a drain on the movie industry's finances since forever.

The development process is also convoluted, since game assets could "spoil" a movie's plot, etc. For example, playing through LEGO Star Wars (Episodes 1 to 3) pretty much spoiled Star Wars: Episode 3 once you got there - I remember LucasArts telling me that screenshots could not be used for a guide until after the movie hit the theaters.

Similarly, James Cameron's Avatar had a rushed development (almost no game balancing) when you opted to play a Na'Vi (instead of trucking it through as an RDA security merc) since your weapons were shit against the RDA war machines.

Frankly speaking, StarBreeze did the Riddick tie-in games well (although Dark Athena was kind of Dead Space Lite, and sans necromorphs), but Riddick: Escape From Butcher Bay and Dark Athena are probably one of the best movie/game tie-ins thus far.

Generally speaking, If I want the stories from video games, I'll just play the game. That said, I'm curious how the Warcraft movie will be. I'm hoping for the best, based on Blizz's track record with cinematics.
